title: assistant-style-mixer scratchpad
content:
Goal: quick experiments for mixing assistant writing styles + guardrails into single prompts. Personal scratchpad — messy, lots of TODOs.

Motivation:
- We often need a single API call that can behave like: concise technical explainer + upbeat product copy + safety-aware fallback.
- Current approach: route to different persona templates or call adapter model. Trying to embed multi-style behavior in prompt few-shot templates to reduce routing complexity.

High-level approach ideas:
1) Layered instructions: top-level goal, then a short 'voice belt' section with 2–3 examples showing style transitions.
2) Few-shot pairs where same input maps to different tone variants, plus selection instruction ("apply variant X unless content touches sensitive topics then use fallback Y").
3) Use LLM's system/assistant chaining (simulate in one prompt) — e.g., first generate candidate variants then apply a filter. More tokens but easier to iterate.

Experiments (mini-corpus):
- domain: API docs + marketing blurbs + user-facing error messages.
- seed inputs: 10 short prompts (see list below).

Seed prompts: ["Explain how Redwood batching reduces per-token cost.", "Short blurb for the pricing page about dedicated capacity.", "Error message: model unavailable during deployment.", "Describe prefix caching to a new engineer.", "One-sentence elevator pitch for enterprise."]

Template A (compact few-shot, aim: 1–2 shots, <= 300 tokens):
- System: "You are a multi-voice assistant. Follow the shot examples. Output only the requested variant."
- Shot 1: Input: "Explain KV cache" -> Variant Tech: "The KV cache stores past key/value pairs to avoid recomputing attention for cached prefixes, reducing compute on repeated contexts."
- Shot 2: Input: "Explain KV cache" -> Variant Marketing: "KV caching speeds up responses and cuts costs by reusing context — great for chat apps and multi-turn flows."
- Instruction: "Given input, produce two labeled variants: [tech] and [marketing]. If input touches privacy/security, prepend [safety-check]."

Quick failures observed (when running against gpt-style toy):
- Hallucination: 'privacy' detection brittle; marketing variant sometimes omits important operational caveats.
- Length drift: marketing variant expands into product roadmap unless constrained by explicit length tokens.
- Style contamination: technical variant picks up marketing adjectives when examples placed too close.

Notes on mitigation:
- Add explicit negative examples in shots ("do not say X").
- Force token limits via inline instruction ("<= 40 words").
- Add a short classifier few-shot at top: examples of "sensitive" vs "not-sensitive" to reduce false negatives.

Template B (two-pass within single request):
1) Pass 1: generate 3 candidate variants with short labels (tech/marketing/concise).
2) Pass 2: run a safety filter instruction that only keeps candidates passing an explicit checklist (no PII, no promises about SLA, no pricing numbers).

Pros: cleaner separation, easier to run internal checks.
Cons: more tokens, latency implications. Need to measure tokens vs cost tradeoff.

Few-shot set idea (compact table in prompt):
- Row format: INPUT || LABEL || OUTPUT
- Provide 4 rows covering: generic explanation, error message, marketing blurb, compliance-sensitive phrasing.
- Then ask: "For X produce outputs for labels: tech | marketing | friendly-error".

Edge-case failures catalog (quick):
- Ambiguous user intent -> assistant produces both a marketing blurb and a technical deep-dive, confusing caller expecting one channel.
- Safety triage misses legalese (eg. 'guarantee' synonyms).
- Implied sensitive content: input mentions "HIPAA" and prompt incorrectly produces example PHI-style text.

Instrumentation + eval plan:
- Create a 100-example testbed spanning categories (doc, marketing, infra alerts, legal).
- Metrics: style precision (does output match requested label), safety recall (# of sensitive flagged correctly), token cost, average latency.
- Simple scoring: two crowd labels per output + automated regex checks for banned terms.

Open TODOs / next steps:
- Build the 100-example testbed (assign to Marcus).
- Try Template A with 3 different models (8-bit quantized variants) and record token usage.
- Add explicit negative example set for 'no promises' and 'no PHI' (Priya).
- Prototype two-pass prompt and measure latency delta.
- Decide whether to keep single-prompt default or route when user-level policy flags present.

Prototype prompt (minimal):
"SYSTEM: You are a multi-voice assistant. See examples."

EXAMPLES:
INPUT: 'How does batching save money?'
[tech] 'Batching aggregates concurrent requests so GPUs compute shared attention in fewer kernel launches, lowering per-token compute.'
[marketing] 'Batching reduces per-response cost by combining requests — lower fees for high-throughput apps.'

TASK: For the INPUT below, return three labeled variants: [tech], [marketing], [concise]. Limit each to <= 40 words. If the input contains privacy, HIPAA, PII, or warranty words (warranty/guarantee), instead return a single [safety-check] explaining why a manual review is needed.

INPUT: "<<USER_INPUT>>"

Quick log of runs: (local toy LLM)
- 2025-11-10: Template A -> style precision 0.67, safety misses 0.12
- 2025-12-03: Template B two-pass -> style precision 0.81, safety misses 0.04, token cost +28%

Reminders to self:
- Keep examples short and sharply distinct.
- Use explicit negative shots for anti-hallucination.
- Add a minimal regex safety-check at app layer as belt-and-suspenders.

Questions for Marcus/Priya:
- Marcus: can you take the testbed creation? Put examples into spreadsheet and tag with category.
- Priya: draft the negative example list for legal/compliance.

Links / refs:
- internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-library/pull/129
- linear: https://linear.app/RED/issue/UX-4121

-----
Notes-to-self (short):
- This is exploratory; likely will split into: 1) production-safe routing, 2) compact in-prompt style variants as fallback.
- Do quick user study with 5 engineers to validate style preference (A/B: single vs routed).

End of scratchpad. Keep messy.
